title: Mooring Systems and Anchors
analyses: Mooring line tension and offset analysis
Mooring line strength and failure analysis
Drag anchor, suction anchor and pile anchor analysis
Mooring system redundancy and line-break analysis

models.text: The suite should implement catenary equations, force and moment equilibrium, elastic cable theory, nonlinear extensible cable formulations, Lagrangian dynamics, Newtonian motion, three-dimensional rod equations, Cosserat rod models, nonlinear finite-element cable formulations, geometric stiffness and tension-only element models.

The suite should include lumped-mass line models, consistent-mass finite-element formulations, distributed hydrodynamic loading, Morison's equation, nonlinear drag, added-mass effects, material damping, hydrodynamic damping, seabed friction, nonlinear contact, snap-tension dynamics and transient wave-frequency and low-frequency mooring response.

Appropriate models include potential-flow diffraction and radiation theory, Cummins' convolution equation, first-order wave excitation, second-order wave-drift forces, quadratic transfer function models, response amplitude operators, six-degree-of-freedom vessel equations, nonlinear restoring forces and time-domain station-keeping simulation.

The suite should include classical bearing-capacity theory, Coulomb earth pressure relationships, Mohr–Coulomb plasticity, undrained shear strength methods, suction anchor capacity models, suction caisson installation and uplift models, drag embedment anchor trajectory models, plate anchor holding-capacity models, pile anchor axial and lateral resistance models, nonlinear soil–anchor interaction and cyclic anchor degradation.

The suite should implement chain and wire fatigue S–N relationships, rainflow cycle counting, Palmgren–Miner damage, probabilistic line tension distributions, extreme value methods, first-order reliability methods, Monte Carlo simulation, line-break transient response, progressive mooring failure models and system-level reliability assessment.

The suite should combine nonlinear finite-element mooring dynamics, potential-flow vessel hydrodynamics, soil–anchor nonlinear response, stochastic environmental loading and reliability modelling. It should also support hybrid quasi-static/dynamic mooring calculation, coupled mooring–riser–hull simulations, numerical–experimental model calibration and digital-twin mooring tension estimation.

inputs.text: Number of lines, line arrangement, anchor coordinates, fairlead positions, line headings, line lengths and water depth.
Chain diameter, wire-rope diameter, synthetic rope diameter, linear mass, axial stiffness, minimum breaking load, drag coefficients and bending stiffness where relevant.
Shackles, connectors, clump weights, buoyancy elements, chain stoppers, fairleads and their certified load capacities.
Displacement, draft, centre of gravity, mass moments of inertia, hull geometry and hydrostatic restoring characteristics.
First-order motion RAOs, second-order drift loads, added mass, damping and wave excitation coefficients.
Wind speed and direction, wave spectra, current profiles, directional combinations and extreme environmental return-period conditions.
Initial pretension per line, installation tension tolerances and selected equilibrium positions.
Anchor type, dimensions, embedment depth, projected area, structural strength and intended loading direction.
Undrained shear strength, friction angle, soil layering, effective stress, cyclic degradation and anchor penetration resistance.
Bathymetry, seabed inclination, contact friction coefficients, seabed stiffness and seabed obstacles.
Simulation duration, time-step control, line hydrodynamic damping, vessel damping and dynamic excitation.
Individual line failure, anchor movement, connector failure, degraded stiffness and partial mooring-system failure.
Wave scatter diagrams, cyclic tension distributions, chain/wire fatigue properties and design service life.
Allowable vessel offsets, line-tension limits, minimum anchor holding capacity, clearance requirements and system redundancy criteria.

subtitle: Static and dynamic mooring analysis, vessel offsets, line fatigue, anchor holding capacity and station-keeping reliability.
ic: The initial conditions shall establish the mooring system geometry, including vessel position, anchor coordinates, fairlead positions, mooring line lengths, catenary shapes and seabed contact regions.

The mooring system shall initially be brought into static equilibrium under line self-weight, buoyancy, pretension and the specified vessel position. The resulting line tensions, anchor loads, vessel offset and line–seabed contact configuration shall form the starting state for dynamic simulation.

For coupled vessel–mooring analysis, the initial vessel displacement, orientation, velocity and angular velocity shall be specified. Initial environmental forcing shall be consistent with the selected equilibrium. Dynamic simulations may start from calm-water equilibrium or from a pre-existing environmental response.

Anchor initial conditions shall include embedment depth, orientation, soil stress, installation disturbance and existing holding-force mobilization where relevant. Fatigue analyses shall include accumulated line damage and the condition of chains, ropes, connectors and fairleads.
bc: At the vessel end, each mooring line shall connect to a prescribed or dynamically moving fairlead. The connection shall transfer the appropriate tensile forces while allowing rotations consistent with the fairlead and line model.

At the anchor end, the boundary shall represent a fixed, elastically restrained or nonlinear soil-supported anchor, depending on the anchor type and required analysis fidelity. Drag anchors, suction anchors and pile anchors shall use suitable soil resistance and capacity conditions.

Along the seabed, the mooring line shall interact through contact, seabed friction, possible embedment and lift-off. Environmental boundaries shall impose current drag, wave-induced motion and other applicable distributed hydrodynamic effects.

The vessel shall be subjected to wind, wave and current forcing, with mooring reactions returned to the coupled vessel model. Pretension shall be established through prescribed line length, winch tension or an equivalent installation condition.

For line-break simulations, the selected line connection or load-carrying capability shall be removed at the specified event time. Snap-loading analyses shall allow transient slackening and re-tensioning. Interference analysis shall account for appropriate line-to-line and line-to-structure clearances or contact.

calibration: Calibration should use measured mooring line tensions, vessel excursion records, anchor load tests, offshore station-keeping observations and laboratory mooring-system experiments.

Mooring axial stiffness and damping should be calibrated using manufacturer-certified chain, wire and synthetic rope tests. Nonlinear load-extension behaviour, hysteresis, creep and cyclic degradation should be represented where relevant to the line material.
Hydrodynamic drag and added-mass parameters should be calibrated using submerged line experiments and measured dynamic line response.
Line–seabed friction and contact properties should be calibrated against controlled chain or rope interaction tests and local seabed soil measurements.
Anchor resistance models should be calibrated using field installation records, instrumented pullout tests, laboratory anchor experiments and site-specific geotechnical investigations.
Vessel hydrodynamic damping and low-frequency motion parameters should be calibrated using measured vessel motions and corresponding environmental conditions.
Fatigue behaviour should be informed by component fatigue tests, chain-link tests, wire fatigue measurements and documented service experience.
Calibration should include representative intact and degraded configurations, while reserving independent failed-line and extreme environmental cases for validation where possible.
verification: Static mooring configurations should be verified using analytical catenary solutions and independently computed line-equilibrium benchmarks.
Line tensions, suspended lengths, seabed contact lengths and anchor loads should satisfy force equilibrium and geometric compatibility checks.
Dynamic mooring models should undergo time-step and line-segmentation convergence studies.
Axial stiffness, damping, line inertia and hydrodynamic force implementations should be checked using single-line controlled test cases.
Seabed contact should be verified for frictional sliding, lift-off, touchdown and contact-pressure behaviour.
Coupled vessel–mooring models should be tested against prescribed vessel motions and independently calculated line tensions.
Anchor holding calculations should be checked against recognized benchmark cases for drag anchors, suction anchors and pile anchors.
Line-break and snap-load simulations should undergo transient convergence checks and consistent energy diagnostics where applicable.
Fatigue calculations and reliability sampling methods should be verified using controlled reference datasets and reproducibility testing.
validation: Line tension predictions should be compared against instrumented full-scale mooring systems or independent physical-model tests.
Vessel offsets, low-frequency excursions and dynamic responses should be assessed using measured environmental and motion records.
Anchor holding capacity should be validated using representative full-scale pullout tests or suitable physical experiments.
Seabed contact behaviour should be compared against measured line touchdown positions, contact movement and friction resistance.
Line-break response should be assessed using controlled experiments or sufficiently documented observed incidents where reliable measurements exist.
Fatigue predictions should be evaluated against independent component fatigue tests and inspection histories.
Station-keeping reliability should be assessed against long-term operational records, documented failures and suitably supported probabilistic evidence.

geometry.text: Catenary mooring lines, taut-leg moorings, chain-wire-rope assemblies, synthetic ropes, drag anchors, suction anchors, pile anchors, clump weights, buoyancy modules, fairleads and seabed-contact regions.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS, DXF and supported DWG should be accepted for anchor bodies, suction caissons, padeyes, shackles, fairleads, chain links, connectors and buoyancy modules.

CSV, XYZ, JSON, XML, DXF three-dimensional polylines, GeoJSON and GML should be accepted for line paths, fairlead coordinates, anchor locations, line segment lengths and mooring layout geometry. The importer should preserve the connection order, line segment type, anchor location, floating-unit reference frame and seabed contact geometry.

geometry.cat: Specialized anchor and foundation geometry formats
geometry.text: IFC where relevant, LandXML, Gmsh MSH, Abaqus INP, Nastran BDF, ANSYS CDB, MED, UNV, VTK/VTU and Exodus should be accepted for compatible anchor structures, suction foundations, soil domains and soil–anchor contact analyses.

STL, OBJ, PLY, GLB, LAS/LAZ, E57, GeoTIFF, ESRI ASCII Grid, XYZ bathymetric surfaces and NetCDF seabed grids should be supported for complex anchor profiles, as-installed seabed geometry, irregular anchor penetration conditions and surveyed mooring corridors.
